title: pH calibration allows accurate glucose detection in interstitial fluid via reverse iontophoresis

paper_content.abstract: Reverse iontophoresis (RI) is a promising non-invasive, wearable technology for the transdermal extraction of interstitial fluid (ISF), which contains rich biomarkers relevant to health status. Despite the advancement of wearable sensors, this technology is still restricted for accurate non-invasive biomarkers detection. The main challenge lies in the instability of ISF extraction during RI. We found that this instability is primarily caused by the skin surface pH variations because of the interaction between the RI-induced H+ movement and the skin recovery ability. Here, we investigated how the skin surface pH affected RI, theoretically and experimentally; and developed a wearable device and a calibration method to enable accurate non-invasive ISF glucose detection, accordingly. The results showed that glucose prediction accuracy was markedly improved, with mean absolute relative difference (MARD) decreased from 34.44% to 14.78% across both healthy and diabetic volunteers.
paper_content.introduction:
With rising living standards and economic progress, personalized diagnostic technologies are gaining increasing attention for their potential in health assessment and early disease diagnosis1–3. These technologies typically involve two critical dimensions and trends: wearable, non-invasive monitoring and accurate prediction of physiological status. The breakthroughs of flexible electronics and nanotechnology in recent years may address the requirements for wearables4,5, however, it is still a big challenge to achieve accurate and non-invasive prediction6. Biomarkers, such as metabolites7–9, hormones10,11, electrolytes12, and proteins13,14, serve as pivotal roles in achieving accurate prediction of physiological status6,15,16. These biomarkers, derived from biofluids such as sweat17–20, tears21, saliva22, urine23, and interstitial fluid (ISF)24–27, have already been explored for wearable and non-invasive health monitoring. Notably, among these biofluids, ISF contains the most categories of biomarkers, and its composition is closely correlated with blood-derived information28,29. Therefore, we think that ISF may be the best choice to achieve accurate and non-invasive biomarker detection.

Non-invasive ISF detection is currently achievable through radiofrequency30, ultrasound31, optics32, metabolic heat conformation33, and reverse iontophoresis (RI)34–37. The former four methods face challenges for accuracy due to indirect measurement and interferences from complex tissue, especially from omnipresent blood38. In contrast, RI provides direct extraction and detection of ISF, holding great potential for accurate analysis of biomarkers24. RI, first introduced by Richard H. Guy’s group in 1989, has undergone significant advancements over the years39. In 2001, Cygnus Inc. launched the GlucoWatch® Biographer, the first and only commercial device based on RI, demonstrating the potential for wearable and non-invasive glucose detection40. Unfortunately, the device was discontinued in 2007 due to several limitations, including skin irritation, sweat-induced interference, discomfort of wearing, measurement inaccuracies from sensor-skin displacement by rigid components, and instability of ISF extraction41. Recent advancements in flexible electronics and nanotechnology have addressed many of these challenges, such as skin irritation42, sweat-induced interference38, and discomfort of wearing5,43–45, reigniting interest in RI for wearable and non-invasive biomarkers detection46–49. Despite these innovations, the issue with accurate detection remains. We found that the key issue lies in the fluctuations of ISF extraction34.

Under the influence of the skin’s physiological negative charge, RI facilitates the transdermal extraction of ISF by applying a mild current to the skin50. This process is driven primarily by the electromigration of cations in the electrical double layer (EDL), thereby making the electroosmotic flow of small neutral biomarkers, for example, glucose51. Here, we found that the EDL at the interface between the skin and the RI electrodes significantly affects this electroosmotic flow. Specifically, the extracted H⁺, along with the release of additional H⁺ from biochemical reactions, collectively lead to changes in the pH of the RI-induced fluid accumulated at the skin surface and within the epidermal electroosmotic microchannel (referred to as the skin surface pH in this study). The skin recovery mechanisms, including natural barriers such as sweat glands and the stratum corneum that maintain homeostasis and prevent excessive polarization52–54, will hinder the change. The interaction leads to the fluctuations of skin surface pH, which changes the zeta potential (ZP) of the EDL55,56, thereby causing instability in the electroosmotic flow of ISF accordingly.

To validate this hypothesis, here we provide a detailed theoretical analysis of how skin surface pH influences ISF extraction by modulating the ZP of keratin, thereby directly affecting ISF extraction and subsequent detection accuracy. We conducted a numerical simulation to elucidate these effects; we designed and fabricated an epidermal electronic device integrating symmetric ISF extraction electrodes, glucose, Na+, and pH sensors for experimental investigation. Theoretical experiments were conducted firstly to validate our hypothesis. Then, a skin surface pH calibration method was developed and validated to enable accurate and non-invasive ISF glucose detection through in-vitro and in-vivo experiments.
paper_content.results:
Theoretical analysis of effect of skin surface pH on RI

Theoretical analysis. Human skin is composed of dermis, epidermis, stratum corneum (SC), and hydrolipid film (HF) that overlay the SC (Fig. 1a). At the interface between the HF and the SC, charge separation occurs due to the interaction of solid and liquid phases. This phenomenon leads to a spatial distribution of potential differences near the interface, thereby establishing the EDL structure, which comprises a Stern layer and a diffusion layer. RI extraction of ISF hinges on two key mechanisms: the electromigration of ions and the electroosmosis of small neutral molecules. The electromigration involves ionic fluxes originating from both the bulk ISF and the diffusion layer. In contrast, the driving force for the electroosmotic transport of small neutral molecules primarily arises from the migration of counterions (carrying charges opposite to the skin surface) within the diffuse layer under an applied electric field. Consequently, the concentration of these counterions governs the electroosmotic velocity (Fig. 1b, Supplementary Note 1).

The skin’s inherent negative charge under physiological conditions results in cation-dominated ion flux (counterions) within the EDL during RI. This cation flux facilitates the movement of small neutral molecules, e.g., glucose, towards the cathode. In this process, Na+ dominates the ion flux and acts as the primary carrier in the EDL, while extracted H+ and released H+ from biochemical reactions at the epidermal interface alter the skin surface pH. Additionally, the skin recovery mechanisms, including natural barriers such as sweat glands and the stratum corneum, help maintain homeostasis and prevent excessive polarization52–54, thereby mitigating the pH changes induced by RI. The interaction between the H+ movement and the skin recovery ability make the fluctuations of skin surface pH. Fluctuations in skin surface pH indeed modulate the charge density of the skin, affecting the quantity of counterions (mainly Na+) in the EDL diffusion layer, which in turn lead to the fluctuations of electroosmosis.

The charge density of the skin can be reflected by the ZP (the potential at the slip plane)55. Particularly, the negative charge of skin originates from the acidic nature of the HF, which is induced by the sweat secretion, sebum degradation, and microbial metabolites57,58. The ionization state of carboxylic groups within the keratin of SC varies with pH, exhibiting a neutral state at the isoelectric point (pI) where the pH ranges from 4 to 4.5, a positive charge state below the pI while a negative charge state exceeds the pI59,60 (Supplementary Fig. 1a). We preliminarily explored the influence of skin surface pH on ZP using keratin (main components of SC), and the results revealed the great influence and a negative correlation between ZP and pH (Fig. 1c, Supplementary Table 1).

Numerical simulation. Here, we use glucose as an example to investigate the impact of pH variations on electroosmotic flow, an ISF extraction model was developed in COMSOL, incorporating ZP measurements across different pH levels (Fig. 1c, Supplementary Note 2 and Supplementary Table 1). Simulation results revealed that at pH 4, the glucose concentration at the anode is higher than at the cathode. Conversely, when the pH exceeds 4, the glucose concentration at the cathode becomes significantly higher than that at the anode, and both electrodes exhibit a rise in glucose concentration as pH increased, aligning with the ZP-dependent extract mechanism by RI (Fig. 1d, e, Supplementary Fig. 1b–h).

Design and characterization of the epidermal electronic device

Design and fabrication of the wearable device. To validate our hypothesis and theoretical analysis, we designed a wearable electronic device accordingly, which incorporated a pair of RI extraction electrodes for ISF extraction, glucose sensors, Na⁺ sensors and pH sensors for fluxes measurement and skin surface pH monitoring. Specifically, the device is divided into two symmetrical sensing regions, Part A and Part B. Each part comprises a semi-circular RI electrode, a glucose sensor, a Na⁺ sensor, and a pH sensor (Fig. 2b). The layer assembly of the device consists of a flexible polyimide (PI) substrate layer, enabling seamless conformity to skin deformations for comfortable wearing; an Ag conductor layer to ensure stable electrical connections; a sensors layer for simultaneous ISF extraction, glucose, Na⁺, and pH detection; a patterned 3M adhesive layer for attachment to the skin and precise hydrogel patterning; and a hydrogel layer serving as the ISF collection reservoir and microreaction chamber (Fig. 2c, d). The epidermal device was fabricated by screen printing, followed by layer-by-layer surface functionalization (Supplementary Fig. 4).

Characterization of the wearable device. We firstly conducted comprehensive characterizations of the proposed device to validate its functionality. Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) and X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) of the electrodes confirm the successful fabrication and functionalization of the device (Supplementary Figs. 6, 7). The detection principle of this device involves two electrochemical mechanisms: an enzyme-catalyzed reaction that converts glucose concentration into amperometric current (i-t) under the applied bias voltage; and a Nernstian response that converts Na+ concentration and pH into potentiometric voltage (Fig. 2a).

H₂O₂, an intermediate product of glucose oxidation, was initially measured to evaluate the performance of the electrodes, which exhibited excellent performance with a sensitivity of 0.44 μA mM⁻¹ (Supplementary Fig. 8). Then, a series of comprehensive tests were conducted on the glucose sensor, including stepwise, sensitivity, consistency, selectivity, and storage stability. Stepwise testing revealed that the steady-state current of the i-t response increased with glucose concentration (Fig. 2e). The glucose sensor exhibited a highly linear response, with a sensitivity of 236.42 nA mM⁻¹ from 0–3 mM (Fig. 2f) and 28.22 nA mM⁻¹ from 3 to 30 mM (Supplementary Fig. 9d). Sensor-to-sensor consistency was well maintained with minimal variation in sensitivity across three devices (Supplementary Fig. 9h). The sensor also demonstrated high selectivity against a range of potential interfering species (Fig. 2g, Supplementary Fig. 9e–g). After 14 days of storage, the sensor retained ~75% of its original sensitivity (Fig. 2h, Supplementary Fig. 9i). Considering that the fluctuations in skin surface pH during RI process affect the performance of the glucose sensor, sensitivity testing was performed under different pH conditions (Fig. 2i, Supplementary Fig. 10e). The relationship between the sensitivity and pH presented as a quadratic curve. At the pH of 7, normal pH of ISF, the sensitivity reached 298.56 nA mM⁻¹ (Fig. 2j). The ultraviolet (UV) absorbance (ABS) of H₂O₂ generated by glucose oxidase (GOx) at varying pH values exhibited a comparable trend in sensitivity (Supplementary Fig. 10a–d), revealing that pH impacts the performance of glucose sensor through diminishing the activity of GOx. Consequently, prior to calculating the glucose concentration through sensitivity, a pH correction for sensitivity is required first, which is essential for accurate glucose detection. The test results for different pH values and glucose concentrations demonstrated that higher glucose detection accuracy was attained after pH correction (Fig. 2k, l, Supplementary Fig. 11). Similar to the glucose sensor, the Na⁺ sensor exhibited robust performance across the testing of step-response (Fig. 2m), sensitivity (52 mV decade⁻¹) (Fig. 2n), stability (Supplementary Fig. 12a), consistency (Supplementary Fig. 12d), selectivity (Fig. 2o, Supplementary Fig. 12c), and storage life (Fig. 2p, Supplementary Fig. 12e). The pH sensor demonstrated excellent outcomes in multiple evaluations: step-response (Fig. 2q, Supplementary Fig. 13c), sensitivity (−52 mV decade⁻¹) (Fig. 2r, Supplementary Fig. 13a), stability (Supplementary Fig. 13b), consistency (Supplementary Fig. 13e), selectivity (Fig. 2s, Supplementary Fig. 13d), and storage life (Fig. 2t, Supplementary Fig. 13f). Utilizing an environment-controlled flexible electronics system (FE-SDT), the device maintained functionality during mechanical deformation, thus making it ideal for wearable applications (Supplementary Figs. 14, 15). These results confirm the robust performance of the proposed wearable device.

Experimental validation of effect of skin surface pH on RI

Na+ flux under different skin surface pH. To further corroborate the hypothesis regarding the influence of skin surface pH on RI, validation experiments were carried out employing a Franz diffusion cell system in conjunction with a Strat-M® membrane to simulate the ISF extraction process (Fig. 3a, Supplementary Fig. 16). Tris-HCl buffer solutions at varying pH levels were added into the receiver chamber to simulate different skin surface pH environments, while NaCl solutions containing glucose were placed in the donor chamber to simulate ISF. Since the extraction process of RI involves the Na+ flux by electromigration and the glucose flux by electroosmosis, and the primary counterions in a physiological state are Na+, the impact of skin surface pH on the Na+ flux was explored firstly. The significant difference in potential response of the Na⁺ sensor in the receiver chamber before and after 15 min of RI extraction clearly confirmed the effective Na⁺ extraction (Fig. 3c). Notably, the extracted Na⁺ flux exhibited minimal variation across different pH levels, confirming that changes in skin surface pH has a negligible impact on the Na+ flux (Fig. 3d, Supplementary Table 3). The reason may be that the electromigration of Na+ predominantly occurs in the bulk solution, while the pH value only affects the Na+ flux in the diffusion layer of the EDL.

Glucose flux under different skin surface pH. Experiments were also conducted to explore the impact of skin surface pH on the electroosmotic extraction of glucose. The i-t responses of the glucose sensor before and after extraction showed a substantial increase in the steady-state current, underscoring the effective glucose extraction (Fig. 3e, Supplementary Figs. 17–22, and Supplementary Table 4). After converting this current difference into the extracted glucose flux, it was discovered that the extracted glucose flux rose progressively as the increasement of skin surface pH. Moreover, higher glucose levels in the subcutaneous ISF at 30 mM (Fig. 3g, Supplementary Fig. 23b) led to greater extracted glucose flux compared to the 15 mM one (Fig. 3f, Supplementary Fig. 23a). The linear regression analysis across the entire pH range 5–10 showed a slope significantly different from zero (p=0.00207 at 15 mM and p=0.01343 at 30 mM) and a high determination coefficient (R²=0.927 at 15 mM and R²=0.817 at 30 mM), indicating a clear overall upward trend in extracted glucose with increasing pH. And the results demonstrated that, in the cases of subcutaneous glucose levels at 15 mM and 30 mM, the extracted glucose concentration was increased by 0.013 mM and 0.027 mM per each 1 pH unit increment, respectively (Fig. 3h). Interestingly, the increase ratios are both ~33%/pH, confirming the uncorrelation between the electroosmotic velocity and the subdermal glucose concentrations. These results verify that skin surface pH affects the electroosmotic flow of glucose significantly, requiring a calibration model to achieve accurate glucose prediction.

Skin surface pH calibration for subdermal glucose prediction

The skin surface pH calibration method presented in this work tackles two crucial aspects: the correction of glucose sensor sensitivity and the calibration of glucose extraction flux (Fig. 3b). The former rectifies the change in enzyme activity resulting from pH variations, which directly influence the performance of the glucose sensor. The sensitivity of the glucose sensor exhibits a quadratic relationship with pH as described by equation (1.10). The latter centers on mitigating the deviations in glucose extraction flux linearly induced by skin surface pH changes. In this RI process, Na+ flux induces glucose flux; therefore, it serves as the base of subdermal glucose prediction, and it also indicates the different skin properties of different person38,61. The comprehensive calibration and subdermal glucose prediction equation is presented as equation (1.25), with detailed derivations in the Supplementary Note 3.

In-vitro evaluation of the calibration method and wearable device

Dynamic changes in glucose and skin surface pH during RI extraction. Capitalizing on the established linear relationship between skin surface pH and glucose extraction flux, we performed in-vitro experiments to appraise the precision of glucose prediction both with and without pH calibration (Fig. 4a, Supplementary Fig. 24). Artificial skin was used in the in-vitro experiments, it was assumed that the physical properties of the skin remained constant during the RI process, thus the Na+ flux would be constant at a certain extraction condition. Therefore, the Na+ flux was not tested here. To minimize errors from repeated ISF extractions, glucose and pH measurements from five consecutive cycles were used for validation. The subcutaneous simulated ISF was a solution containing 140 mM NaCl with glucose concentrations of 6, 12, 18, 24, and 30 mM, respectively. The in-vitro testing findings of this device were categorized into three segments: Part A, Part B, and the overall test results. When the subcutaneous glucose concentration was 12 mM, the steady-state current of the i-t responses acquired from Part A and Part B increased significantly over the five consecutive RI extractions (Fig. 4b, e, Supplementary Figs. 30, 31). Simultaneously, the skin surface pH detected by the pH sensors in both parts exhibited significant fluctuations (Fig. 4c, f, Supplementary Figs. 30, 31). The extracted glucose concentrations were linearly fitted against the extraction times of RI. Herein, the slope (denoted as Slope 1) derived from the regression represents the extracted glucose by a single instance of RI. Notably, after applying pH calibration, the slope 1 for Part A and Part B exhibited a marked increase, with the Slope 1 for Part A augmenting by 8.1% (Fig. 4d) and that for Part B growing by 7.5% (Fig. 4g). The different increase between the Part A and Part B may be caused by the different changes of electrical property at the interface of artificial skin and electrodes. The increase reflects the suppressive effect of declining skin surface pH on glucose flux during consecutive RI cycles, which is essential for subsequent prediction of subcutaneous glucose concentrations. The extraction results at subdermal glucose concentrations of 6 mM (Supplementary Figs. 28, 29), 18 mM (Supplementary Figs. 32, 33), 24 mM (Supplementary Figs. 34, 35), and 30 mM (Supplementary Figs. 36, 37) were also recorded and analyzed (Supplementary Table 4).

Relationship between extracted and subcutaneous glucose concentrations. A linear fit of the extracted glucose (represented by the fitted slope 1) against the subcutaneous glucose concentrations revealed a consistent positive linear correlation (denoted as slope 2) for both Part A and Part B of the device (Supplementary Fig. 38). The Slope 2 serves as the foundation for subsequent subcutaneous glucose prediction in the experiments. The results showed that following pH calibration, the Slope 2 exhibited an increment, with an increase of 12.1% in Part A and 6.2% in Part B of the device (Supplementary Fig. 38). To achieve higher-frequency measurements, which are of great importance for practical wearable applications, the measurements from Part A and Part B are combined to obtain the overall results (Supplementary Fig. 27). The results further confirmed the linear relationship with 9.9% increase of slop after pH calibration (Fig. 4h), underlining the impact of pH calibration on subsequent glucose prediction.

Subcutaneous glucose prediction using the calibration method and wearable device. After obtaining the relationships of extracted glucose to simulated subcutaneous glucose with and without pH calibration, we performed RI extraction and detection on additional solutions with pre-determined subcutaneous glucose concentrations. Specifically, solutions with subcutaneous glucose concentrations of 5 mM, 8 mM, 12 mM, 18 mM, and 25 mM were individually subjected to our experimental procedures. The results demonstrated a substantial elevation in glucose prediction accuracy after pH calibration, with the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) decreased markedly from 11.2% to 2.9% (Fig. 4i). This improvement highlights the efficacy of skin surface pH calibration in reducing the inaccuracies caused by pH fluctuations during RI. These experiments serve as a preliminary validation of the proposed skin surface pH calibration method and device.

In-vivo evaluation of the calibration method and wearable device

To further validate the applicability of the wearable device and the pH calibration method in practice, oral glucose tolerance tests (OGTT) were performed on 6 healthy participants and 15 Type Ⅱ diabetic patients (Fig. 5a). During the 2.5-h experiment, fluctuations were observed in the extracted glucose flux, skin surface pH, and Na⁺ flux. The slight fluctuations in Na⁺ extraction are likely attributable to changes in skin permeability induced by prolonged RI extraction38. These three curves showed abrupt changes between consecutive data points throughout the test, which were attributed to the alternating polarity of ISF extraction (Fig. 5b, c left, Supplementary Fig. 39). Glucose prediction accuracy was evaluated under various calibration conditions: without calibration, with Na⁺ calibration only, and with cooperative Na⁺ and pH calibration (Fig. 5b, c right, Supplementary Fig. 39). The results showed that after cooperative calibration, the glucose prediction curve closely aligned with the reference curve. Clarke’s error grid analysis of healthy participants demonstrated a progressive increase in the percentage of data points falling within zone A: from 56.67% without calibration to 58.34% with Na⁺ calibration (61.54% reported by Pu et. al.38), and 78.33% with cooperative Na⁺ and pH calibration (Fig. 5d, g, Supplementary Table 6). The results of diabetic patients showed that the percentage of data points falling within zone A and B: from 70% without calibration to 90% with cooperative Na⁺ and pH calibration (Fig. 5h, k, Supplementary Table 6). Mean absolute relative difference (MARD) of healthy individuals further corroborated this trend, significantly decreasing from 25.49% (without calibration) to 20.04% (Na⁺ calibration) and 10.91% (cooperative calibration) (MARD≤20% by FDA) (Fig. 5g). The results of diabetic patients showed that MARD was changed from 42.11% (without calibration) to 33.24% (Na⁺ calibration) and 18.10% (cooperative calibration) (Fig. 5k). Following cooperative calibration, the MARD observed across all volunteers was 14.78% (Supplementary Fig. 41). These results indicate that skin surface pH calibration plays a vital role in accurate predication of subdermal glucose based on RI, especially for prolonged extraction. The results also highlight the potential of the developed device and the proposed pH calibration method as a wearable and non-invasive tool for continuous biomarkers monitoring.
paper_content.methods:
Materials
Glucose, sodium chloride (NaCl), potassium chloride (KCl), calcium chloride (CaCl₂), ascorbic acid (AA), uric acid (UA), dopamine (DA), Nafion solution, polyimide (PI) film, keratin azure (K8500), glucose oxidase (GOx), polyvinyl butyral (PVB), poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene)-polystyrenesulfonate (PEDOT:PSS), and platinum nanoparticles (PtNPs) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (Shanghai, China). Chitosan (CS), poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC), industrial-grade multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs), glacial acetic acid, glycerol, Na⁺ carrier X, sodium tetrakis[3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)phenyl] borate (Na-TFPB), dioctyl sebacate (DOS), Hydrogen Ionophore I (Tridodecylamine), potassium tetraphenylborate (KTClPB), cyclodextrin (CYC), Polyvinyl butyral (PVB), Pluronic F-127, and carbinol were prepared by HEOWNS (Tianjin, China). Deionized water (DI), phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH 7.2–7.4), and tris(hydroxymethyl) aminomethane (Tris)-HCl buffer were prepared by Huaying Prosperous Technology Co., Ltd. (Tianjin, China). All reagents were of analytical grade and used without further purification. Polyimide (PI) film was purchased from Leviathan Technology Co., Ltd (Tianjin, China). Ag/AgCl ink was supplied by Sun Chemical Co., Ltd. (UK). Prussian blue-doped carbon (PBC) ink and Ag conductive ink were provided by Gaintzor Electronic Technology Co., Ltd. (Qingdao, China). Medical adhesive tape (3M-2477P) was acquired from 3M Medical Materials & Technologies (USA). Connectors (65801-008LF) were purchased from Amphenol (USA). Franz diffusion cells were purchased from Shanghai Chemical Laboratory Equipment Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Strat-M® membranes (47 mm disks, 300 μm thickness) for transdermal ISF extraction were obtained from EMD Millipore Corporation (Billerica, USA). The TPY-2 transdermal diffusion apparatus was purchased from Huanghai Pharmaceutical Testing Instruments Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China) for precise temperature control and magnetic stirring of the ISF. A constant current source (ZF-9, Shanghai Zhengfang Electronic & Electrical Co., Ltd.) was used to provide a 150 μA cm⁻² current density for RI extraction. All electrochemical characterizations were performed with an electrochemical workstation (CHI 660E, Shanghai Chenhua Instrument Co., Ltd.).

Fabrication and preparation of the wearable device
Screen printing process. The fabrication process of the device is depicted in Supplementary Fig. 4. Firstly, the surface of the PI film (50 μm thickness) was cleaned using an alcohol wipe to remove surface contaminants. After cleaning, the PI substrate was subjected to O₂ plasma treatment (TS-PL10MA, Shenzhen Tonson Tech Automation Equipment Co., Ltd.) to eliminate organic impurities and enhance the surface’s hydrophilicity. This treatment was carried out under radio frequency power of 300 W, with a flow rate of 100 mL min⁻¹ for 90 s. The treatment resulted in improved surface hydrophilicity (Supplementary Fig. 2), which is critical for subsequent electrode printing and functional modification. Electrodes were printed on the treated PI substrate using a screen-printing method (420 mesh screen, HP-AL series, Shanghai Xuanting Screen Printing Equipment Co., Ltd.), which was performed in a layer-by-layer process. The initial step was printing an Ag conducting layer on the PI substrate, which was essential for ensuring good electrical conductivity. Then an Ag/AgCl layer was deposited on the Ag conducting layer, serving as the ISF extraction electrode and, importantly, the reference electrode (RE) for the glucose, Na⁺, and pH sensors. Finally, a PBC layer was added to function as the working electrode (WE) for the glucose, Na⁺, and pH sensors, thus completing the construction of this screen-printed electrodes fabrication. Each printed layer was cured at 120°C for 3 min to ensure adequate adhesion and functionality. Non-sensing areas were encapsulated using a waterproof, skin-adhering, double-sided acrylic medical adhesive tape (3M-2477P, USA). The patterned structure of the sensor was realized by employing laser engraving technology using the Universal VLS2.30 Laser System (USA). The operation parameters were set as follows: a power level of 80%, a speed of 30%, and the laser engraving process was repeated three times to enable subsequent Functional modification.

GOx membrane solution preparation. GOx lyophilized powder (10 KU, Sigma) was dissolved in 555 μL of PBS to prepare a GOx solution with a concentration of approximately 100 mg mL⁻¹. This solution was then diluted to obtain a final concentration of 10 mg mL⁻¹. To prepare the chitosan precursor solution for embedding GOx, 10 mL of DI was added to 0.1 g of chitosan (1 wt%), followed by the addition of 30 μL of glacial acetic acid (0.3 v/v%) and 1 mL of glycerol (10 v/v%). The mixture was heated at 80°C and stirred for 2 h. Subsequently, 0.1 mL of PtNPs aqueous solution was incorporated to complete the chitosan precursor solution. The prepared GOx solution (10 mg mL⁻¹) was mixed with the chitosan precursor solution in a 2:1 volume ratio to yield the GOx membrane solution, which was stored at 4°C for future utilization.

Na+ and H+ selective membrane solution preparation. The Na+ selective membrane solution was prepared by dissolving 2 mg of Na+ carrier X (97%), 1 mg of Na-TFPB (97%), and 131 mg of DOS in 708 μL of CYC, ensuring complete dissolution. Afterward, 66 mg of PVC was added and ultrasonicated for 30 min to achieve a homogeneous solution, forming the Na+ selective membrane solution. For the pH sensor selective membrane, the Na+ carrier was replaced with Tridodecylamine and the Na-TFPB was replaced with KTClPB, while the other steps and ratios remained unchanged.

Preparation of reference membrane solution for Na+ and pH sensors. The reference membrane solution for both the Na+ and pH sensors was prepared by dissolving 0.2 mg of MWCNTs, 2 mg of pluronic F-127, 79.1 mg of PVB, and 50 mg of NaCl in 1 mL of anhydrous methanol. MWCNTs, F127, and NaCl were first dissolved in methanol to form a uniform solution, with NaCl reaching saturation. Following this, PVB was added to the mixture and ultrasonicated for 20 min to ensure complete dissolution of PVB. The final reference membrane solution was stored at 4°C to ensure adequate stabilization prior to use.

Modification process of the functional layer. A 1 μL aliquot of the GOx membrane solution was individually applied to the WE on both Part A and Part B of the glucose sensors. The solution was left to naturally solidify at room temperature for 30 min. Subsequently, a 1 μL aliquot of PEDOT:PSS aqueous solution was separately applied to the WE on both Part A and Part B of the Na+ and pH sensors. The solution was allowed to solidify at room temperature for 1 h, thereby forming a conductive polymer layer. A 1 μL aliquot of Na⁺ selective membrane solution was subsequently applied to the WE of the Na⁺ sensors, while a 1 μL aliquot of H⁺ selective membrane solution was applied to the WE of the pH sensors, both on Part A and Part B of the device. The electrodes were then allowed to dry at room temperature for 4 h. Finally, a 30 μL aliquot of Nafion (5 wt%, Sigma) was diluted with alcohol to a 1 wt% concentration and applied to both part A and part B of the prepared device. After curing at room temperature for 1 h, the device was fully prepared and stored at 4°C for preservation. Structurally, each part comprises a semi-circular Ag/AgCl electrode for RI extraction, a glucose sensor with a PBC WE and a quarter-circular Ag/AgCl RE, a circular PBC WE for the Na⁺ sensor, a circular PBC WE for the pH sensor, and a shared quarter-circular Ag/AgCl RE for both the Na⁺ and pH sensors. The detailed structure of the electrode is shown in Supplementary Fig. 3.

Activation process of the device. To ensure stable potential measurements of the ion sensor and eliminate errors caused by baseline drift, the Na+ and pH sensors were immersed for 2 h in a Tris-HCl buffer solution at pH 7 containing 0.1 mM NaCl for activation prior to in vivo testing.

Characterization of the wearable device
Electrochemical characterization of the glucose sensor. All electrochemical tests were conducted using the CHI660E electrochemical workstation. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) scans were performed within the voltage range of −0.6 V to +0.6 V in 1× PBS (0.01 M, pH=7.2–7.4), with a scan rate of 0.1 V s⁻¹. H₂O₂, an intermediate product of glucose oxidation, was first measured to assess the performance of PBC WE. Typically, the WE requires CV scans to remove surface impurities and identify the optimal bias voltage, which was found to be −0.1 V (Supplementary Fig. 8a, b). CV scans at different scan rates showed a linear relationship between peak current and the square root of the scan rate, confirming that the H₂O₂ reaction is diffusion-controlled (Supplementary Fig. 8c, d). For H₂O₂ and glucose testing, the i-t curves were carried out for 60 s, with the steady-state current recorded at the 60-s mark. Stepwise testing revealed a good linear response between sensor current and H₂O₂ concentration (Supplementary Fig. 8e), with linear sensitivity of 441 nA mM⁻¹ observed ranging the 0–5 mM (Supplementary Fig. 8f). The glucose sensor testing follows a similar procedure as H₂O₂, with an initial CV scan determining the optimal bias voltage of −0.1 V (Supplementary Fig. 9a, b). CV results at different scan rates also showed a linear correlation between peak current and the square root of the scan rate, confirming that the glucose reaction is diffusion-controlled (Supplementary Fig. 9c). Therefore, the current can be linearly fitted to concentration using the Cottrell equation. The sensitivity of glucose within the range of 3–30 mM is 28.22 nA mM⁻¹ (Supplementary Fig. 9d). The selectivity of the glucose sensor was assessed by immersing the glucose sensor into a 10 mL Tris-HCl solution at pH 7.4 (Fig. 2g, Supplementary Fig. 9e, f, g). Starting at 100 s, glucose (0.5/5 mM), NaCl (14/140 mM), KCl (0.4/4 mM), CaCl₂ (0.25/2.5 mM), uric acid (0.01/0.1 mM), dopamine (0.01/0.1 mM), ascorbic acid (0.01/0.1 mM), fructose (0.1/1 mM) and glucose (1/10 mM) were sequentially added every 60 s. The solution was stirred continuously for 1 min to facilitate stability before each detection.

The enzyme activity of GOx was evaluated by measuring the concentration of H₂O₂ generated by GOx-catalyzed glucose at different pH values. The reaction mixture consisted of glucose oxidase (10 mg mL⁻¹) and glucose solutions (10 mM) in a 1:1 v/v ratio (prepared in Tris-HCl buffer), incubated for 1 h before measurement The UV ABS test was based on the Trinder’s reaction for H₂O₂, where a standard curve for H₂O₂ concentration was obtained by measuring UV ABS at 500 nm (Supplementary Fig. 10a). A solution of 0.2 mM phenol and 0.2 mM 4-AAP in PBS buffer, along with 0.25 mg mL⁻¹ HRP solution, were prepared for testing. Different concentrations of H₂O₂ (10 mM, 20 mM, 30 mM, 40 mM, 50 mM) were added to the reaction mixture, followed by 500 μL of HRP solution. The mixture was shaken for 5 min at 200 rpm using a shaking incubator (SK-L180-S, DLAB). The reaction solution was transferred to a microplate for analysis using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay reader (Feyond-300, Hangzhou Aosheng Instrument Co., Ltd). The UV ABS at 500 nm for different H₂O₂ concentrations was plotted to obtain the standard curve (Supplementary Fig. 10b, c). The fitting results of the ABS of H₂O₂ and pH value also show a quadratic function curve, which is similar to the relationship between glucose sensitivity and pH, demonstrating its effectiveness (Supplementary Fig. 10d).

Electrochemical characterization of the Na+ and pH sensors. The Na⁺ and pH sensors, based on open circuit potential (OCP), were measured over a duration of 60 s, with the steady-state voltage taken at the 60-s mark. The selectivity of the Na⁺ sensor was evaluated by immersing the Na⁺ sensor into a 10 mL Tris-HCl solution at pH 7.4 (Fig. 2o, Supplementary Fig. 12c). Starting at 100 s, various substances were sequentially added every 60 s, including NaCl (50 mM), KCl (4 mM), CaCl₂ (2.5 mM), uric acid (0.1 mM), dopamine (0.1 mM), ascorbic acid (0.1 mM), glucose (5 mM), fructose (1 mM) and NaCl (200 mM) were sequentially added every 60 s. The selectivity of the pH sensor was assessed by immersing the pH sensor into a 10 mL Tris-HCl solution at pH 6.6 (Fig. 2s, Supplementary Fig. 13d). Starting at 100 s, NaCl (140 mM), KCl (4 mM), CaCl₂ (2.5 mM), uric acid (0.1 mM), dopamine (0.1 mM), ascorbic acid (0.1 mM), glucose (5 mM), fructose (1 mM) and Tris-HCl buffer (pH 7.6) were sequentially added every 60 s. Prior to each test, the solution was continuously for 1 min to facilitate the stability of all substances added to the reaction system.

Mechanical evaluation of the wearable device. The fabricated wearable device was evaluated using an environment-controlled flexible electronic testing system (FE-SDT, SINOAGG, Beijing). This testing included measurements of the resistance of the RI electrodes before and after bending, as well as electrochemical performance tests of the sensors under different bending conditions. The bending test consisted of two phases: the bending process and the recovery process, which together formed a complete cycle. The bending limit was set to 50% of the sensor’s flexibility (approximately 90°), with a waiting time of 10 s once the limit was reached. The resistance testing during the bending process was conducted over two cycles (Supplementary Fig. 14). To evaluate the stability of electrochemical performance, the device was tested for the steady-state current of glucose, the steady-state voltage of Na⁺, and the steady-state voltage of pH after undergoing different numbers of bending cycles (0, 10, 30, 50, and 100 bends) (Supplementary Fig. 15). These tests allowed for a comprehensive assessment of the sensor’s mechanical performance and its ability to maintain stability under wearable applications.

Experimental validation of effect of skin surface pH on RI
Given the challenges presented by uncontrollable factors, including human skin temperature, skin impedance, and ISF flow rate, experiments were employed to exclusively evaluate the impact of skin surface pH on RI. The ISF extraction and testing system was constructed using Strat-M® transdermal membranes (47 mm in diameter, 300 μm in thickness) to simulate human skin. A Franz diffusion cell setup was employed, with the donor and receiver compartments designed to mimic the ISF extraction process. The receiver chamber contained 3 mL of Tris-HCl buffer solution at varying pH levels (ranging from pH 5 to 10). Commercial Ag/AgCl electrodes were used as the RI electrodes to minimize ISF extraction fluctuations related to electrode degradation during RI. A constant current source was applied, delivering a 0.5 mA current for 15 min to facilitate the ISF extraction (Supplementary Fig. 16). Firstly, we assessed the effect of varying skin surface pH on Na+ extraction flux. The donor chamber in the Franz cell contained 15 mL of Tris-HCl buffer solution with 140 mM NaCl and either 15 mM or 30 mM glucose at pH 7.4. Then we investigated the influence of skin surface pH on glucose extraction flux. This experimental setup provided a controlled environment to evaluate the pH-dependent changes in RI.

Preparation of the in-vitro ISF extraction and testing system
Due to the interference of uncontrollable factors such as skin temperature, skin impedance, and interstitial fluid flow rate, the effect of pH as a single variable on glucose extraction flux was investigated through in vitro simulation experiments. Figure 4a, Supplementary Fig. 24 illustrates the setup of the system, which includes a constant current source to supply the RI extraction current, a TPY-2 intelligent transdermal diffusion instrument to maintain a constant temperature of 37 ± 0.1°C, and a magnetic stirrer to simulate ISF flow. The Strat-M® transdermal membrane (47 mm diameter, 300 μm thickness) mimics human skin, while two electrochemical workstations (CHI660E) are used to measure glucose concentration, Na+ concentration, and pH on the membrane surface. A switch controls the ISF extraction and detection process automatically, and a computer is used for data acquisition and processing. RI is set as 150 μA cm⁻² for 3 min for one extraction cycle, which is selected for subsequent glucose extraction testing.

To reduce fluctuations in ISF extraction induced by electrode degradation, alternating current polarity was utilized between consecutive extractions (Supplementary Figs. 25, 26). This approach helped maintain the performance of RI electrodes and ensured more stable extraction conditions. To further minimize potential errors from repeated ISF extractions, glucose and pH measurements from five consecutive cycles were selected for validation, providing a more reliable dataset for assessing extraction consistency and the accuracy of glucose predictions.

OGTT Procedure
The OGTT data collection process is illustrated in Fig. 5a. After attaching the prepared device to the skin, a 10-min warm-up was initially conducted to ensure tight adhesion of the device to the skin and stabilize the RI current. Following this, glucose, Na⁺, and pH are sequentially measured in both parts of the device; subsequent measurements follow the same protocol. After the initial measurements, ISF is extracted for 3 min, with the extraction direction set from Part B to Part A. Measurements are then repeated, with the first set of valid data labeled as Datapoint 1. The polarity is then switched to obtain subsequent data points, such as Datapoint 2, Datapoint 3, and so on. The time lag between blood glucose and ISF glucose is established as 10 min, consistent with commonly reported physiological lags62,63 (Supplementary Table 8).

After an 8–14 h fasting period, 6 healthy volunteers and 15 diabetic patients participated in a 3-h OGTT. Participants consumed a 250 mL bottle of glucose solution containing 75 g glucose over a 5-min period. Blood glucose levels were measured using a commercial glucometer (ACCU-CHEK, Switzerland) for healthy volunteers and venous blood sampling points for diabetic patients as the reference. The experimental setup included the fabricated epidermal device, a constant current source, electrochemical workstations, a switch circuit, and a laptop. A wearable device was applied to the participants’ forearm for continuous glucose, Na+, and pH detection, with RI performed at a current density of 150 μA cm⁻² for 3 min for one extraction cycle. After each extraction cycle, glucose, Na+, and pH levels were measured for one minute. The polarity of the RI current was alternated between successive cycles to reduce the consumption of RI electrodes. The performance of the proposed skin surface pH calibration method was evaluated by comparing the predicted blood glucose levels with reference measurements using Clarke’s error grid analysis.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors present an intriguing wearable, non-invasive device designed for clinical-level detection of interstitial fluid biomarkers by leveraging pH-calibrated reverse iontophoresis. This approach is innovative, particularly as it addresses the longstanding issue of extraction instability due to variations in skin surface pH. While the work undoubtedly pushes the frontier in biosensing technology, several critical issues must be addressed before the manuscript can be considered for publication in Nature Communications.
1. Zeta Potential Measurements: In supplementary Table 1, the standard deviations for the zeta potential (ZP) measurements of keratin across different pH levels are alarmingly high relative to the mean values. This level of uncertainty impedes a confident assignment of positive or negative charges, especially at lower pH values, and undermines the assertion presented in Fig. 1d regarding a pronounced negative correlation between ZP and pH. A re-evaluation of these uncertainties, along with a more robust statistical treatment or additional replicates where possible, would strengthen this aspect of the study.
2. Glucose Concentration Discrepancy (Lines 105–107 vs. Fig. 1f): The manuscript states that glucose concentrations at the anode are higher at low pH compared to high pH (Lines 105–107), yet Figure 1f does not appear to corroborate this claim. The authors must reconcile these differences by either adjusting the text or providing a thorough explanation that accounts for the observed data trends. It is crucial to clarify whether this discrepancy stems from experimental variability, calibration issues, or another underlying phenomenon.
3. Rationale for Glucose Concentration in Figure 2g: The selection of a 5 mM glucose concentration for the experiments depicted in Figure 2g is not adequately justified, particularly since Figure 2f employs a much lower concentration range (0– 300 µM). The authors should clarify the rationale behind these differing concentration regimes and explain their relevance to the overall experimental design and clinical applicability.
4. Absence of Error Bars in Key Figures: Figures 2h, 2p, and 2t currently lack error bars, which are indispensable for assessing the reliability and reproducibility of the presented data. Including error bars will provide insights into the variability and statistical confidence of the measurements, thereby bolstering the study's credibility.
5. Inconsistency in Sodium Concentration Ranges: The experimental design utilizes sodium concentrations in the range of 10–200 mM, yet Figure 3d shows extracted sodium concentrations in the micromolar range. This apparent inconsistency warrants a detailed explanation—potentially involving differences in extraction efficiency, calibration protocols, or inherent sample dilution effects—to ensure that readers can clearly follow the experimental logic.
6. Anomalous Electrode Current Response: In Figure 8b, the Prussian Blue-modified electrode exhibits a simultaneous increase in both anodic and cathodic currents in the presence of hydrogen peroxide. This dual response is unexpected and remains unexplained by the current discussion. A more detailed analysis or additional experiments to elucidate this phenomenon would greatly enhance the manuscript’s mechanistic insights.
7. Statistical Validity of pH-Dependent Results: The overlapping standard deviation ranges depicted in Figures 3f–h call into question the conclusion that the results at pH 7–10 are distinct. The authors should either perform a more rigorous statistical analysis to substantiate this claim or reconsider the interpretation of these data points.
8. Correction of Supplementary Figure 37 Axis Labels: The glucose concentration axis labels in Supplementary Figure 37 appear to be misrepresented. Correcting these unit labels is essential for the clarity and accuracy of the supplementary data.
9. Clarification of Extraction Time for Figure 4g: Figure 4g presents glucose concentration values derived from an extraction process, but the specific time interval used for this extraction is not indicated. Including this detail is necessary for reproducibility and for a proper understanding of the extraction kinetics.
10. Sodium Flux versus pH Inconsistency: Lastly, the manuscript (Lines 335–336) asserts that sodium flux decreases with increasing pH; however, the trend in Figure 3d does not consistently support this claim. The authors are encouraged to re- examine the data trend, provide additional analysis, or revise their conclusion accordingly

Comments to Authors on the paper
Abstract
Lines 12-15. These 2 sentences are quite difficult to understand. Is 'instability' defined/explained anywhere in the paper? Is H+ flux ever measured, and what is the skin self-recovering from, exactly?
Lines 15-17. There is a sensing of pH by the device created, but is it really measuring skin 'surface' pH, or rather the pH of whatever medium is present adjacent to the pH sensor?
Introduction
Lines 52-54. At pH 7, the physiological concentration of Na+ is about 133 mM, while that of H+ is 10-4 mM. Even though H+ is a very mobile ion, it seems to me that the more than 106-fold difference in concentration between Na+ and H+ means that the former will be do the "heavy-lifting" in terms of carrying current across the skin during RI. This should be the case even if the pH falls to 6 or 5 (and we know that by pH 4 the net negative charge on the skin has been neutralised (or even reversed) and the EOF switches to the opposite direction).
Lines 56-57. Reference 52 is incomplete and is a paper about wound healing. It does not appear to say very much of relevance to the self-recovery mentioned in the abstract associated with application of RI.
Results & Discussion
Lines 79-82. RI applies a fixed current, so the charge flowing between the electrodes must be matched by the charge carried by ions in the 'in vivo' part of the circuit. This will involve all available charge carriers with the distribution between them being determined by their mobilities and concentrations.
Lines 85-87. I'm not sure that anyone has measured this proton flux or shown that it changes skin surface pH. Incidentally, what is meant by skin surface pH in this context? Without introducing some water on the surface, how is a measurement of pH performed? Without water, what does pH "of the surface" even mean?
Lines 87-88. Another statement for which there is no experimental evidence as far as I know. What 'self-recovery' mechanism is invoked here, exactly?
Lines 89-91. It is true that experiments ex vivo where it has been possible to change the pH of solutions on either side of the membrane have shown that lowering the pH from 7.4 to that equal to the isoelectric point of the membrane, and then further to below this value, have first reduced electroosmotic flow and the reversed it. But given the ISF pH of ~7.4, the available [H+] is really small and it's hard to envisage that the flux will be able to substantially alter the surface pH (whatever that means - see earlier comment).
Lines 93-94. Characterization of this "hydrolipid film" (HF) would be helpful... What is its nature when a conductive hydrogel is placed between the RI electrodes and the skin? How is its pH chosen and how - if at all - does this pH change with time with or without application of a RI current? Are the changes the same or different under anode and cathode? Do they reverse when the polarity of the electrodes is switched between extractions to prevent depletion/build-up of AgCl?
Lines 105-107. This is all "old news", surely? See comment in S.I.
Lines 118-120. More 'old news' here - the advantages of using this approach were identified by Cygnus more than 30 years ago!
Lines 122-127. So, do I understand correctly that the pH sensor is detecting the value in the gel near the electrode surface? Is this not near where glucose is converted to gluconic acid (releasing H+ locally)?
Fig. 1c. Presumably, the regions labelled as high and low pH cannot be ISF, as the pH there must be fixed. The figure needs to be more clearly drawn.
Fig. 2k and 2l. Difficult to assess the relevance of some of this characterisation work performed in the pH range of 5-10. Yes, it's indeed possible that glucose detection is influenced over this range, but surely this does not occur in vivo? So, the more important question is 'over what range does [glucose] vary in a typical RI extraction-detection use of the device?'
Line 177. A more objective assessment of performance would be better!
Lines 178-180. But are you really measuring skin "surface" changes in pH here, as opposed to changes in the bulk pH of the hydrogel?
Lines 204-206. This is not a widely accepted model for mammalian skin so data obtained using it must be treated with caution and scepticism. The experiment has been done before, in essence, using mammalian skin so why repeat it here using an artificial membrane?
Fig. 3. There is really nothing new here except that EO flow can occur across a charged membrane when an electric field is applied. More flow will occur in the direction of counterion movement as the charge on the membrane increases. The flux of a water-soluble, unionised species present in the solvent will be proportional to its concentration, all other factors being the same.
Lines 226-228. Again, no surprise here. Na+ flux is driven principally by electromigration, far more than by EO. It's the major positive ion current/charge carrier in the system, so it's obvious that its flux will be insignificantly affected by pH.
Lines 244-246. This is well-known as has been reported multiple times before. However, as we do not know the extent to which the charge on a (real) skin membrane in vivo changes during the use of an RI device, there is no basis for concluding that a pH-based correction is needed to ensure that accurate deductions about the glucose levels in the ISF are being made.
Lines 255-257. How does it do that? As Na+ is the principal charge carrier and RI is done under constant current conditions, one expects (and it's true) that the sodium flux per unit current per unit time is actually quite constant, and this has been shown in vitro and in vivo in man. So how can JNa+ be "at the base of subdermal glucose prediction"?
Line 261. Sub-heading does not make complete sense.
Lines 272-276. The system is symmetrical so why are the i-t responses different in Figs. 4b and 4e, and why are the pH fluctuations different (Figs. 4c and 4f), both in absolute values and the extent of change of pH - less than 0.1 unit in Part A, more than 0.2 unit in Part B? These don't seem to be massive changes in pH in any case and the impact as reported in Figs. 4d, 4g, 4h and 4i confirm that this is the case. The "explanation" offered in this paragraph is not convincing, to say the least (mostly, because it does not explain anything!).
Lines 295-297. Exactly how were the data from Parts A and B combined?
Lines 298-300. The data in Fig. 4h show a decent correlation between extracted glucose and subdermal glucose both with and without pH 'calibration'. It would be good to see confidence intervals on the slopes and to test whether they are significantly different. In a practical sense, it seems unlikely that the differences in slopes would dramatically impact on the clinical value of the data when one adds in the pH correction.
Fig. 5. [1] Are the units of extracted glucose correct in 5b and 5c? Should this be micromolar? [2] In the same panels, pH is increasing from about 6 to 10, the latter likely to cause some skin irritation, no? What is causing the increase in alkalinity? Why does the pH change in a sawtooth manner for the normal volunteer but not for the person living with T2D? The fluctuation in predicted glucose levels is more sawtooth for the diabetic patient (whose pH is not varying like that) than that for the normal patient (whose pH is up-and-down throughout) How (in)consistent was that behaviour?
Methods
Line 512. I don't believe that this sensitivity can be measured to an accuracy of 8 picoAmps (the 3rd decimal place here)!
Comments to the authors on the Supplementary Information
Lines 30-31. How do you know this as a fact? Based on what evidence, exactly?
Lines 38-39. Which is which? Whatever is the phase on the skin surface, it is hard to describe it as liquid...
Lines 59-60. Same statement as above but does not obviously flow from what is written here which appears to be standard, accepted dogma.
General remark on Suppl. Note 2. OK, not really anything terribly new or controversial here, it seems. The bottom line appears to be that EO flow depends on the charge on the membrane and that the latter depends on the pH of the 'liquid' phases on either side. The premise, therefore, appears to be that, if one can control the pH of the 'liquid' phase on the skin surface, one can be sure that EO flow will be fixed during RI and that the glucose detected in the 'receiving' gel will therefore be proportional to that in the ISF.
Line 121. The data from which this empirical equation is derived was acquired over a very wide - and non-physiological - range of pH, so its relevance to the 'real world' is not established. What is the form of the relationship when the range of pH values is limited to something sensible/realistic?
Line 124. And the electroosmotic component? Missing?
Lines 142-146. I’m not sure that I would write the equation like this. The units of uglu are velocity. The product {A x uglu} is therefore equivalent to the EO volume flow rate induced by the imposition of the electric field across the charged skin membrane. It seems to me that {A x uglu} must have the same value for all small, neutral molecules present in the system - how can it be specific to glucose?
General remark on Suppl. Note 3. So, at the end of the day, the approach used requires measurements in the sensor gel of glucose, Na+ and pH. Ref 22 in the SI used Na+ as an 'internal standard', effectively to correct for how the charge on the skin may vary from person to person and hence how EO flow would be affected as a result. Did the authors check to see if the approach outlined here, without considering the impact of small changes in pH, would work just as well? If the answer is no, then they probably should...
S.I Fig. 10. On many graphs, using stronger colours for the datapoints and the lines connecting them would be helpful.
S.I Fig. 10. Why are dependencies so different as a function of concentration at different pH values? I'm not sure I'd want a sensor on my arm that led to a pH of 9 or 10...
S.I Fig. 13b. Impossible to see data on this panel.

S.I. Fig. 26. Impossible to see bars in the "Data point 1" and "Data point 3" boxes.
S.I. Fig. 27. Minimal variation in pH here…
S.I. Fig. 29. Again difficult to understand the manner in which pH varies over extraction times.
Same comment on S.I. Figs, 30, 31, 32, 34, 35.
S.I. Fig. 32. But what happened in panel g?
S.I. Fig. 37. Makes more sense to use the same y-axis scale for these two graphs. The correlations between glucose extracted and subdermal glucose are pretty good with or without pH calibration, it seems to me. I'd like to see confidence intervals on the slopes and whether the with and without pH calibration values are significantly different or not.
S.I. Fig. 38. Would be helpful if the data for the healthy volunteer were shown using the same y-axes for extracted glucose, Na+ and pH. Similarly for the diabetic subject. Please use bolder colours to facilitate visualisation. Why are the sawtooth variations prominent in some curves but not others?

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This manuscript is an excellent addition to the literature. The authors have identified a pain point in the development of on-body iontophoretic devices and have provided an innovative solution for it. Polarity switching to minimize current instability is a notable feature of the proposed device design to mitigate skin irritation. Moreover, the proof of concept of pH fluctuation as well as the establishment of a solution via calibration is commendable.
While I suggest that the manuscript be accepted for publication, certain aspects can be included in the discussion section, which can help delineate the relevance and practicality of the designed device:
1. Is there any lag or delay in the physiological status of markers in blood versus their effect in ISF? Can you please provide some references to this aspect?
2. In relation to my first question, is this lag (if any) different for different markers, hence making such a device more suitable for certain biomarkers (such as glucose) more than others? Essentially, can this same device be used for any biomarker, or will the calibration or other aspects be specific to a single biomarker?
3. A major drawback of iontophoretic devices is the risk of local skin burns due to electric current itself, or trips in the device due to non-ideal contact with high conductance fluids for example: accidental water contact. Can you please discuss or suggest any potential safety features that can be embedded in the on-body device, which will break the circuit and arrest the device before a current overload takes place?
4. How did the authors arrive at the glucose range of 6 to 30 mM for the in vitro testing? Can you please provide a correlation of the tested ranges with blood glucose levels in humans? In addition, can you provide some information about the quantitation limits of the developed device?
5. Did the authors make several of these devices and if yes, what was the variability observed across different devices in terms of calibration and sensitivity to skin pH changes? If some discussion on this can be added, it will improve the robustness of the proposed model/device.

Authors have made detailed responses to my comments but have not, in my opinion, provided compelling evidence that the addition of pH monitoring represents a true step-change in the use of reverse iontophoresis for glucose monitoring. Specific remarks follow:
1. Authors have accepted that they nmeasure a bulk pH in the fluid on the skin surface; they do not measure the flux of H+ ions. Relatedly, the authors now state that the pH measured is the same as that in the "epidermal electroosmotic microchannel" but how do they know this, given that they cannot actually measure what is going on in that space?
2. Authors also accept that they do not know the quantitative contribution that H+ makes to carrying the applied current across the skin. They acknowledge that it must small (given the very low concentration of H+ ions available to do so) and this - by extrapolation - challeges their premise that correcting for the amount of H+ around is needed.
3. Authors' definition of 'skin recovery' remains vague. Imposing an electric field across a membrane drives in ions and causes membrane impedance to decrease; when the field is removed, ions will diffuse out down the created concentration gradient and impedance returns to its original value... is this recovery or just physics?
4. Authors' responses refer repeatedly to H+ changes being due to "extracted H+" (which cannot be very much from a physiological fluid like the ISF that has a pH close to neutral) and "released H+" from 'biochemical reactions' at the epidermal interface. What are these reactions and how much H+ do they release? Can they really be sufficient to cause the local pH to increase to 10?
5.The response about the hydrolipid film is obscure and quickly digresses to discuss the mysterious "epidermal electroosmotic microchannel"...
6. Authors state without any 'back-up' or verification that any contribution to H+ presence resulting from the enymatic reaction between glucose and glucose oxidase is small compared to H+ extraction in the EOF. Is the Gox reaction the "biochemical reactions" referred to in previous and other answers, or are there others (and, if yes, then what are they)? Either way, the authors need to be up-front here.
7. It's quite difficult to come up with an explanation for pH increasing to 10 during a short period of reverse iontophoresis without some undesirable electrochemistry occurring that results in water electrolysis...
8. This reviewer remains unconvinced about the relevance of the artificial membrane experiments.
9. It remains unclearas to whether the addition of a pH correction, in addition to that achievable with the Na+ correction, provides any real-world added-value in terms of accuracy/prediction given that - except perhaps in very extreme cases as the Authors acknowledge - the pH variation possible is really quite small and unlikely to affect EOF. New Figures R3/R4 support this point of view.
10. This reviewer's concerns about Figure 5 are not assuaged by the Authors' reply which is highly speculative and not supportd by any hard facts.
11. The term "reverse ions" is unusual. I think the Authors mean 'counterions', i.e., ions with a charge opposite to that of the skin.
12. I think that maintaining a pH of 10 on the skin for very long will typically cause visible irritation.

Reviewer #2:
Response: Thank you for your detailed and rigorous comments of our work. We have carefully reviewed each of your concerns and have made substantial revisions to the manuscript accordingly. Below, we provide detailed point-by-point responses to your comments.
Comments to Authors on the paper
Abstract
1. Lines 12-15. These 2 sentences are quite difficult to understand. Is 'instability' defined/explained anywhere in the paper? Is H+ flux ever measured, and what is the skin self-recovering from, exactly?
Response: Thank you for your valuable comments. We acknowledge that our original phrasing lacked clarity and failed to fully define key terms.
In this work, “instability” refers to the fluctuations in the volume and composition of electroosmotic flow (EOF) of interstitial fluid (ISF) during reverse iontophoresis (RI). The instability leads to a dynamic changed relationship between the extracted analyte concentrations and those in subcutaneous ISF, for example, glucose.
For the H⁺ flux, we apologize for the inaccurate description. Exactly, we did not measure the H⁺ flux directly. We measured the pH of the entire microfluid at the skin surface and within the epidermal electroosmotic microchannel throughout the RI extraction process (Fig. R1). The pH changes are primarily due to the movement of H⁺, which have high mobility and is one of the earliest migrating species during the RI process 1. And the pH changes at the skin surface and in the epidermal electroosmotic microchannel affect the skin’s zeta potential (ZP) and consequently influence the flux of the entire EOF.
The skin exhibits a natural resistance to RI-induced ISF extraction, which we refer to as “skin self-recovery”. This encompasses the skin’s ability to buffer pH fluctuations and regulate fluid loss through its structural and physiological barriers, such as the stratum corneum and sweat glands 2-4. These self-regulating responses can suppress the accumulation of extracted ISF and mitigate the extent of local acid-base imbalance caused by RI.
References:
Fig. R1 Schematic of RI-induced electroosmosis flow and extracted fluid at the skin surface and in the epidermal electroosmotic microchannel.
Changes: We have replaced “H⁺ flux” with “H⁺ movement” throughout the text. Additionally, we have further updated on the relevant description of “instability” and “skin’s self-recovery”. Fig. R1 has been added to Supplementary Fig. 5a. For your convenience, we included the revised text here:
“The interaction leads to the fluctuations of skin surface pH, which changes the zeta potential (ZP) of the EDL 55, 56, thereby causing instability in the electroosmotic flow of ISF accordingly.” (Lines 61-63 in the revised Manuscript)
“Specifically, the extracted H⁺, along with the release of additional H⁺ from biochemical reactions, collectively leads to changes in the pH of the RI-induced fluid accumulated at the skin surface and within the epidermal electroosmotic microchannel (referred to as the skin surface pH in this study).” (Lines 56-59 in the revised Manuscript)
“The skin’s self-recovery mechanisms, including natural barriers such as sweat glands and the stratum corneum that maintain homeostasis and prevent excessive polarization 52, 53, 54, will hinder the change.” (Lines 59-61 in the revised Manuscript)
2. Lines 15-17. There is a sensing of pH by the device created, but is it really measuring skin 'surface' pH, or rather the pH of whatever medium is present adjacent to the pH sensor?
Response: Thank you again for your comment regarding the pH sensing in our system. We acknowledge that our initial phrasing of skin surface pH did not convey the intended meaning.
As stated in the response to Comment 1, the term “skin surface pH” in this study refers to the pH of the entire microfluid at the skin surface and within the epidermal electroosmotic microchannel throughout the RI extraction process (Fig. R1). We refer to this measured value as “skin surface pH” in the manuscript.
